title: Breathing in harm: current insights into the effects of air pollution on cardiorespiratory health

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Breathing in harm: current insights into the effects of air pollution on cardiorespiratory health》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · section-2-p3】We aimed to critically examine the mechanisms through which air pollution contributes to cardiopulmonary and systemic diseases, with a particular focus on cardiovascular morbidity, chronic respiratory disorders, and vulnerable populations such as children, pregnant women, and individuals with pre-existing conditions. This review is distinguished from others by integrating recent evidence on air pollution and coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) interactions, highlighting international differences in air quality standards, and discussing the most recent updates to exposure limits. Furthermore, it emphasizes emerging mechanistic insights and evaluates mitigation strategies at both policy and individual levels. By consolidating these perspectives, this review aims to provide a comprehensive, evidence-based framework that shows the significance of air pollution as a global health crisis and identifies critical directions for future research and policy.

【Introduction · section-2-p1】Climate significantly affects air quality, with factors such as pollutant emissions, transportation, and dispersion influenced by temperature, humidity, wind patterns, and vertical mixing.1 Climate change is expected to worsen air quality in densely populated areas by altering atmospheric circulation, precipitation patterns, and chemical processes.2 Air pollution is defined as the presence of chemical and biological substances in the atmosphere that may pose risks to human health and the environment.3 Based on that, air pollution consists of a complex and dynamic mixture of PM, gases and gaseous co-pollutants, whose composition and sources can vary significantly across locations and over time.34 The major conventional air pollutants used to quantify exposure firstly include particulate matters (PMs), which are classified into coarse (PM10, mean aerodynamic diameter 10–2.5 μm), fine (PM2.5, 2.5–0.1 μm), and ultrafine (PM0.1, < 0.1 µm) particles based on size.5 Gaseous pollutants include nitrogen monoxide (NO), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), sulfur monoxide (SO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and carbon monoxide (CO), as well as volatile organic compounds such as benzene, acrolein, and butadiene. PM10 is typically generated from mechanical activities like industrial processes, mining, and construction, whereas PM2.5 mainly results from the combustion of fossil fuels, biomass, and crop residue burning. Ultrafine particles and volatile organic compounds are largely attributed to fresh emissions from motor vehicles.6 Motor vehicles and industrial facilities are also major sources of gaseous air pollutants, particularly nitrogen oxides (NOx), which are primarily generated through the high-temperature combustion of fossil fuels. These processes occur in engines, power plants, and manufacturing operations, where elevated temperatures facilitate the reaction between atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen, resulting in the formation of NO and NO2.7 While SO2 primarily originates from fossil fuel combustion, particularly from automobile exhaust.8 Ozone (O3) is the most common secondary pollutant, formed through photochemical reactions, and exists in both gas and particle phases along with various inorganic and organic acids.9

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Breathing in harm: current insights into the effects of air pollution on cardiorespiratory health》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Studies in patients with cardiovascular disease, heart failure and circadian syndrome · section-14-p1】Evidence shows that HF-related hospitalizations increase significantly with air pollution exposure, and this rise is greater than that observed for other chronic diseases. This supports a strong link between air pollution and both the exacerbation of HF symptoms and heightened vulnerability among individuals living with HF.185 Yang et al.186 by performing an updated systematic review and meta-analysis, reported that CO had the strongest link to HF events (3.46% increase per 1 ppm), followed by SO2 (2.20%) and NO2 (2.07%) per 10 ppb. O3 was also positively associated (0.95% per 10 ppb). PM2.5 and PM10 were both significantly linked to HF, with 1.29% and 1.30% increases in hospitalization or death per 10 μg/m3, respectively.

【Studies in patients with cardiovascular disease, heart failure and circadian syndrome · section-14-p2】In a large UK Biobank cohort of 48,850 individuals with circadian syndrome, long-term exposure to various air pollutants, including PM2.5, PM10, PM2.5 absorbance, NO2, NOx, and an overall air pollution score, was significantly associated with major CVD subtypes.50 Interestingly, PM2.5 was linked to increased risks of coronary heart disease, HF, and stroke, PM2.5 absorbance was associated with HF, NO2, NOx, and the air pollution score were associated with increased risk of coronary heart disease, atrial fibrillation, HF, and stroke. Over a 12-year follow-up, 12,570 CVD cases were documented, while multistate regression models revealed that per-interquartile range increases in pollutant levels were linked to elevated hazards for transitions from circadian syndrome to CVD and from CVD to death.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Breathing in harm: current insights into the effects of air pollution on cardiorespiratory health》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Potential Linking of Air Pollution to Cardiovascular Mortality and Cardiometabolic Risk · section-3-p1】The precise mechanisms underlying the cardiovascular system’s heightened sensitivity to air pollution remain incompletely understood but may be partly explained by its direct interface with pulmonary air or its relatively limited detoxification capacity compared to organs like the liver or lungs.18 Although the lungs are the primary site of particle deposition, inhaled pollutants can exert harmful effects on distant organs, such as the heart and blood vessels, through several interrelated pathways (Figures 1 and 2). Proposed mechanisms include: (1) the release of biological mediators, such as inflammatory cytokines and potentially unidentified signaling molecules, from the lungs into the systemic circulation, (2) activation of sensory receptors in the alveoli that trigger neural reflexes and alter autonomic nervous system activity or stimulate endocrine responses, and (3) the direct translocation of particles or their chemical constituents into the bloodstream, where they may directly impair cardiovascular function. These pathways are not mutually exclusive and are often interconnected, with inflammation and oxidative stress serving as central amplifiers of cardiovascular injury across mechanisms.19

【Impact of PM2.5 as a standalone exposure · section-5-p4】Short-term exposure to PM2.5 levels over hours to days has been shown to trigger cardiovascular events, hospital admissions, and even mortality.3637 The most pronounced associations between PM2.5 exposure and heart failure (HF) have been observed on the same day of exposure, highlighting its role in the acute exacerbation of HF symptoms. This risk appears to be even more pronounced in heart transplant recipients, likely due to their heightened physiological vulnerability.38 In contrast, long-term exposure over months to years is associated not only with a higher risk of major adverse cardiovascular events39404142 but also with the accelerated progression of underlying conditions, such as atherosclerosis.41 Interestingly, regarding the long-term effects of PM2.5 exposure on cardiovascular outcomes, Hayers et al.43 found that each 10 µg/m3 increase in PM2.5 was associated with a 16% higher risk of ischemic heart disease death and a 14% higher risk of stroke death. Moreover, increased cardiovascular mortality was evident even below the current US PM2.5 standard of 12 µg/m3, indicating adverse effects at lower exposure levels. A meta-analysis by Alexeeff et al.44 has observed that a 10 µg/m3 increase in PM2.5 has been associated with a 23% higher risk of ischemic heart disease mortality, 24% higher cerebrovascular mortality, 13% increased risk of incident stroke, and an 8% increase in incident myocardial infarction. However, the latter was not statistically conclusive. More recently, Wang et al.45 noticed that among US Medicare participants, long-term exposure to low levels of PM2.5 (< 9 μg/m3), NO2 (< 75.2 µg/m3), and warm-season O3 (< 88.2 μg/m3) was positively associated with higher rates of stroke-related hospitalizations. These associations were observed in three-pollutant models that accounted for correlations among co-occurring air pollutants and controlled for unmeasured confounding using negative control exposures.

sections.title: 图表阅读
sections.text:
《Breathing in harm: current insights into the effects of air pollution on cardiorespiratory health》：图表的原始标题与说明。

【Figure 1 · mgr.MEDGASRES-D-25-00201-F1】Figure 1 Potential mechanisms of PM exposure on cardiovascular disease mortality.Direct pathways involve PM inhalation, oxidative stress, pulmonary inflammation, and endothelial dysfunction, leading to cardiovascular events. Indirect pathways occur when PM components cross the lung barrier, enter the systemic circulation, and induce systemic inflammation, ultimately contributing to increased cardiovascular mortality. Created with Microsoft PowerPoint and Adobe Photoshop. PM: Particular matter; PM0.1: ultrafine PM (mean aerodynamic diameter < 0.1 μm); PM10: coarse PM (mean aerodynamic diameter 10–2.5 μm); PM2.5: fine PM (mean aerodynamic diameter 2.5–0.1 μm).

【Figure 2 · mgr.MEDGASRES-D-25-00201-F2】Figure 2 Integrated mechanistic pathways from inhalation to cardiovascular injury.Air pollutants initiate oxidative stress and inflammation that drive systemic inflammation, autonomic imbalance, and direct translocation of particles, ultimately leading to cardiovascular injury and disease. Created with Microsoft PowerPoint and Adobe Photoshop. ANS: Autonomic nervous system; BP: blood pressure; CRP: C-reactive protein; HF: heart failure; HPA: hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal; HRV: heart-rate variability; MI: myocardial infarction; NO2: nitrogen dioxide; O3: ozone; PM: particulate matter; PM0.1: ultrafine PM (mean aerodynamic diameter < 0.1 μm); PM10: coarse PM (mean aerodynamic diameter 10–2.5 μm); PM2.5: fine PM (mean aerodynamic diameter 2.5–0.1 μm); SO2: sulfur dioxide; UFP: ultrafine particle; VOC: volatile organic compound.

【Figure 3 · mgr.MEDGASRES-D-25-00201-F3】Figure 3 The linking of air pollution–induced particulate matter and lung dysfunction, COPD, and lung cancer.PM triggers immune activation and oxidant-mediated damage, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and airway remodeling. These processes promote inflammation, activation of the NF-κB pathway, and stimulation of macrophages and epithelial cells. The combined effects result in lung tissue damage, chronic airway remodeling, COPD progression, and, ultimately, increased risk of lung cancer.
